questions.question: What is a Bounded Context in Domain-Driven Design and why does it matter?
questions.title: Bounded Context — What It Is and Why It Matters
questions.direct_answer: A Bounded Context is an explicit boundary within which a particular domain model applies and has consistent meaning. The same word (e.g., 'Customer') can mean entirely different things in different Bounded Contexts — in Sales it is a prospect, in Shipping it is a delivery address, in Support it is a ticket holder. Bounded Contexts prevent the corruption of a single model by keeping each model focused and internally consistent.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands that models are context-specific and that trying to build one unified model across the entire enterprise is a failure mode
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking a Bounded Context is just a microservice — many developers equate the two, but a Bounded Context is a design concept and can be implemented as a module in a monolith
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the relationship between Bounded Contexts and Ubiquitous Language — each BC has its own language, and translation happens at the boundary

sections.title: The Unified Model Trap: Why One Model Per Enterprise Always Fails
sections.content:
In any enterprise of meaningful size, different departments use the same business terms to mean fundamentally different things. Sales calls a "Customer" someone with a lead score and assigned representative. Shipping calls a "Customer" a delivery address with packaging preferences. Support calls a "Customer" a ticket holder with an SLA tier. The natural instinct is to build one `Customer` class that serves everyone — and this is precisely how domain models become incoherent.

Eric Evans introduced Bounded Contexts to solve this. A Bounded Context draws an explicit boundary around a cohesive model where every term has one precise meaning — the **Ubiquitous Language** of that context. "Customer" in the Sales context is a different class with different behavior than "Customer" in the Shipping context, and that is correct by design. The duplication across contexts is intentional: it is far cheaper than the coupling a unified model creates.

The misunderstanding that trips most developers in interviews is equating Bounded Contexts with microservices. A Bounded Context is a **design boundary**, not a deployment decision. A well-structured monolith can contain multiple Bounded Contexts as separate packages or modules. You decide the model boundaries first and the deployment strategy second. Microservices often align with Bounded Contexts, but they are not the same concept — and conflating them leads to premature decomposition.

sections.title: The Linguistic Firewall: How Ubiquitous Language Defines the Boundary
sections.content:
The Bounded Context exists because language is inherently ambiguous across organizational boundaries. Within a single context, the team — developers and domain experts together — agrees on precise definitions for every domain term. These definitions live directly in class names, method signatures, event names, and test descriptions.

When the Sales team says "qualify a customer," the code reads `customer.qualify(QualificationCriteria criteria)`. When Support says "escalate a customer," the code reads `customer.escalate(EscalationReason reason)`. These are different classes in different packages, and the language itself is what marks the boundary. When you find that the same word requires a different vocabulary to describe its behavior, you have crossed into a different Bounded Context.

This linguistic isolation eliminates an entire category of bugs: **miscommunication bugs**. A developer reading the Sales context and seeing `Customer.qualify()` has zero ambiguity about whether this method touches shipping preferences or support tickets. The model is self-documenting because the language constrains it. Translation between contexts happens explicitly — through domain events carrying only identifiers and value objects, through Anti-Corruption Layers, or through shared IDs — never by importing another context's domain class.

sections.title: Beyond Microservices: Implementing BCs in Monoliths and Modular Systems
sections.content:
In a Java monolith, each Bounded Context maps to a top-level package — `com.company.sales`, `com.company.shipping`, `com.company.support` — each with its own domain model, repository interfaces, and application services. The critical discipline is preventing cross-context imports of domain classes.

ArchUnit enforces this at build time with a single rule that fails the build if someone imports across boundaries.

```java
@ArchTest
static final ArchRule salesDoesNotDependOnShipping =
    noClasses().that().resideInAPackage("..sales..")
        .should().dependOnClassesThat()
        .resideInAPackage("..shipping..");
```

This catches the most common corruption vector: a developer importing a class from another context because "it already has the fields I need." Java 9+ modules (`module-info.java`) provide even stronger encapsulation by making internal classes invisible across module boundaries at compile time.

For inter-context communication within a monolith, Spring's `ApplicationEventPublisher` carries domain events between contexts without compile-time coupling. The Sales context publishes `OrderSubmittedEvent` with primitive identifiers and value objects — never a reference to a Sales domain class. The Shipping context subscribes and creates its own `Shipment` aggregate using its own model.

sections.title: Data Ownership: Why Each Context Needs Its Own Tables
sections.content:
Each Bounded Context should own its database tables, even within a shared database. Sales has `sales_customers` with lead scores and opportunity columns. Shipping has `shipping_customers` with addresses and delivery preferences. The data is duplicated by design — because the two contexts need structurally different views of the same real-world concept.

Cross-context queries go through published interfaces or events, never through direct table joins. If Shipping needs the customer's name from Sales, it receives that name as part of the `OrderSubmittedEvent` payload and stores it locally. This means Shipping functions even if the Sales module is temporarily unavailable or undergoing a schema migration.

This data discipline pays off during microservice extraction. Each context already owns its data and communicates through events. Extracting a context into a separate service means moving its tables to a new database and replacing the in-process event publisher with Kafka — the domain model and application logic stay unchanged. Teams that skip data isolation in the monolith phase discover that microservice extraction requires a painful, risky data migration that could have been avoided.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **One Bounded Context, one precise language** — "Customer" in Sales and "Customer" in Shipping are different classes with different fields; they are not the same entity with nulls
- **The unified model trap** — forcing all contexts into one `Customer` class produces constant merge conflicts, nullable fields for irrelevant context, and team coupling
- **Code boundary = package or service boundary** — no cross-context imports of domain classes; communication through domain events, APIs, or ACL adapters
- **Context ≠ Microservice** — a monolith can have multiple Bounded Contexts enforced through packaging; microservices are one deployment strategy for bounded contexts, not the only one
- **Subdomain (problem space) vs Bounded Context (solution space)** — the business has subdomains whether you model them or not; a Bounded Context is your explicit design decision about where a model applies

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
A Bounded Context is an explicit boundary within which a particular domain model applies — inside that boundary, every term has one precise meaning. Outside it, the same word may mean something completely different. DDD makes this boundary a first-class design artifact rather than hoping everyone agrees on a shared universal model.

**The unified model trap**
- In any non-trivial organization, Sales calls a "Customer" a lead with a pipeline score; Shipping calls a "Customer" a delivery address with packaging preferences; Support calls a "Customer" a ticket holder with an SLA tier — the same word, three incompatible models
- Forcing these into one `Customer` class produces a model that satisfies nobody — it grows every field any team ever needed, most of which are null in most contexts
- The trap: the universal model becomes a source of constant merge conflicts, ambiguous field names, and team-level coupling

**What the Bounded Context boundary means in code**
- Each context has its own model classes, its own database schema or collection, and its own Ubiquitous Language — `Customer` in the Sales context and `Customer` in the Shipping context are different classes with different fields
- Communication between contexts happens through explicit integration patterns — domain events, ACL adapters, API contracts — not through shared entity classes or a shared database table
- In microservices, a Bounded Context often aligns with a service — but a monolith can have multiple Bounded Contexts through strict package boundaries and no cross-context imports

**Bounded Context vs Subdomain**
- A Subdomain is a problem-space concept — "Inventory is a subdomain of our e-commerce business" — it's how the business is carved up in reality
- A Bounded Context is a solution-space concept — the design boundary where you implement a model for that subdomain; ideally one-to-one, but legacy or third-party systems may force misalignment

The Bounded Context is not just a naming convention — it's the container for a specific language, a specific model, and a specific team's ownership.

questions.question: What is the difference between an Entity and a Value Object in DDD?
questions.title: Entity vs Value Object in Domain-Driven Design
questions.direct_answer: An Entity has a unique identity that persists through changes in state — two Orders with the same items are not the same Order if they have different IDs. A Value Object has no identity; it is defined entirely by its attributes — two Money objects with the same amount and currency are interchangeable. Value Objects are immutable; Entities are mutable over their lifecycle.

interviewer_intent.testing: Fundamental DDD literacy — this distinction drives key design decisions about immutability, equality, and how to model the domain
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Making everything an Entity with a Long id field, rather than recognizing that many concepts (Money, Address, DateRange) are naturally Value Objects
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Demonstrate with concrete Java code using records for Value Objects and explain the JPA implications of the entity/value object distinction

sections.title: Identity Continuity vs Attribute Equality: The Design Decision That Shapes Everything
sections.content:
Most developers default to slapping a `Long id` and `@Entity` on every class in their domain. This produces a database-centric model where Money has a primary key, Address has a primary key, and DateRange has a primary key — none of which represent real domain identity. The result is unnecessary database tables, pointless joins, and a domain model that reflects the ORM's needs rather than the business's concepts.

The Entity/Value Object distinction exists to prevent this. An **Entity** has a continuous identity through time — your bank account remains "your account" even after deposits and withdrawals change its balance. The identity (the account number) is what matters, not the current state. A **Value Object** is a measurement or description — a price, an address, a date range. It has no identity; it is defined entirely by its attributes. Two `Money` objects representing fifty US dollars are completely interchangeable — there is no meaningful distinction between "this fifty dollars" and "that fifty dollars."

This distinction cascades into everything: how you implement `equals()` and `hashCode()`, whether the class is mutable or immutable, how it maps to JPA, and whether it gets its own database table. Getting this right at the modeling stage eliminates entire categories of bugs and complexity. Conversely, getting it wrong — modeling Money as an Entity with a database-generated ID — creates phantom identity where none exists and forces unnecessary joins for what should be an embedded column group.

sections.title: Entity vs Value Object: The Complete Decision Matrix
sections.content:
| Aspect | Entity | Value Object |
|---|---|---|
| **Identity** | Has unique ID — identity persists through state changes | No identity — defined entirely by attribute values |
| **Equality** | By ID: `order1.id.equals(order2.id)` | By all attributes: same amount + currency = same Money |
| **Mutability** | Mutable — state changes through domain methods | Immutable — replaced wholesale, never modified in place |
| **Java idiom** | Class with identity field and controlled mutation | `record` or final class with no setters |
| **JPA mapping** | `@Entity` with `@Id` — owns its database table | `@Embeddable` — columns embedded in the owning entity's row |
| **Thread safety** | Requires synchronization if shared across threads | Inherently thread-safe due to immutability |
| **Sharing** | References must be managed carefully (aliasing risk) | Safe to share freely — immutable objects cannot be corrupted |
| **Lifecycle** | Independent — persists in its own right | Dependent — exists within or alongside an entity |

sections.title: The Modeling Litmus Test: When to Reach for Each
sections.content:
The decision between Entity and Value Object comes down to one question: **does this concept have a lifecycle that matters to the business?**

- **Use an Entity** when the business tracks it over time, assigns it an identifier, and cares about its history — Order, Customer, BankAccount. Changing the balance doesn't make it a different account; the identity persists through state changes.
- **Use a Value Object** when the business treats it as a replaceable descriptor — Money, Address, DateRange, Quantity. Changing the price on a line item doesn't mean you have a "different price" with its own history — you simply have a new value.
- **Quick diagnostic**: would the business ever say "give me Money number 47"? If no, it is not an Entity. If the concept could be replaced wholesale without breaking any business rule, it is a Value Object.
- **Over-entity-ification warning**: automatically giving everything a `Long id` and `@Entity` is the most common DDD mistake. Money, Address, and DateRange have no real domain identity — forcing one on them adds database complexity where none is needed.

sections.title: Java Implementation: Records for Value Objects, @Embeddable for JPA
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Entity = identity that survives state changes** — bank account is still yours after deposits; `equals()` on the ID field, not attribute values
- **Value Object = interchangeable by attribute equality** — two `Money(100, "USD")` are the same thing; implement as Java `record` for automatic value-based equality and immutability
- **Immutability is the rule for Value Objects** — when the price changes, create a new `Money`; mutable Value Objects introduce "which copy got updated?" bugs
- **Forcing an ID on a Value Object is a model distortion** — `Address` with a primary key treats addresses as persistent entities; use `@Embeddable` or separate JPA and domain classes
- **Most concepts are Value Objects, not Entities** — `Money`, `Address`, `DateRange`, `Email`, `PhoneNumber`, `Quantity` — overuse of Entity (slapping `Long id` on everything) is the most common DDD mistake

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The distinction between Entity and Value Object is about identity — specifically, whether identity is something that persists through state changes, or whether it doesn't matter at all. Getting this distinction wrong produces unnecessary database joins, generated primary keys on objects that don't need them, and a domain model that doesn't reflect how the business actually thinks.

**Entity — identity that survives change**
- An Entity is identified by its ID, not by its current attribute values — a bank account is still "your account" after every deposit changes the balance; what matters is the continuity of identity
- In Java, two Entity instances with the same ID are equal regardless of field differences — `equals()` and `hashCode()` are implemented on the identity field, not on all attributes
- Entities have lifecycle: they are created, modified, and possibly deleted — each state transition is meaningful and may raise a domain event

**Value Object — identity by attribute equality**
- A Value Object has no identity of its own — two `Money(100, "USD")` instances are completely interchangeable; there's no meaningful distinction between "this hundred dollars" and "that hundred dollars"
- Value Objects should be immutable — if the price changes, you create a new `Money` instance rather than mutating the old one; immutability eliminates the "which copy got updated?" class of bugs
- In Java, implement Value Objects as `record` classes — records provide value-based `equals()` and `hashCode()` automatically, and are immutable by default

**JPA implications and the separation strategy**
- JPA requires `@Entity` with a primary key — this works fine for domain Entities, but forcing a primary key onto a Value Object (`Money`, `Address`, `DateRange`) is a model distortion
- The clean solution: store Value Objects as `@Embeddable` columns in the owning entity's table, or as a separate `OrderLineEntity` that is a JPA detail — the domain `OrderLine` remains a Value Object
- Alternatively, separate the JPA entity from the domain object entirely — `OrderEntity` (infrastructure) and `Order` (domain) are different classes mapped by an adapter

questions.question: What is an Aggregate and Aggregate Root in DDD, and what are the design rules?
questions.title: Aggregate and Aggregate Root — Rules and Design
questions.direct_answer: An Aggregate is a cluster of domain objects (Entities and Value Objects) treated as a single unit for data changes. The Aggregate Root is the single entry point — all interactions with the cluster must go through the root, which enforces invariants across the whole aggregate. External objects may only hold references to the Aggregate Root, never to internal objects.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of aggregate boundaries, why they exist (invariant enforcement), and the practical rules that keep aggregates maintainable
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Making aggregates too large — e.g., including Customer inside Order — which creates consistency conflicts and performance problems
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain aggregate sizing heuristics (small aggregates), eventual consistency between aggregates, and reference by ID instead of object reference

sections.title: Why Aggregates Exist: The Consistency Problem Nobody Designs For
sections.content:
Consider an `Order` with several `OrderLine` items. The order's total must always equal the sum of its line prices. A line item cannot exist without its parent order. An order cannot be submitted if it has no lines. These are **invariants** — rules that must hold true after every state change, without exception.

Without aggregates, any code in the system can reach into the `OrderLine` list, add an item, and never recalculate the total. A developer in a hurry directly modifies line quantities through a repository and accidentally breaks the order's consistency. The invariants exist, but nothing enforces them — they rely on every developer remembering every rule, every time.

The Aggregate pattern solves this by creating a **transactional consistency boundary**. All objects that must be immediately consistent after a change are grouped into an aggregate. A single object — the **Aggregate Root** — serves as the gatekeeper: all external interaction goes through it, and it enforces every invariant before allowing the change. Outside code cannot reach past the root to modify internal objects directly.

The design tension that separates experienced DDD practitioners from beginners is aggregate **sizing**. The instinct is to build large aggregates that contain everything related to an order — the customer, the products, the payment history. This creates lock contention, loading performance problems, and merge conflicts. The discipline is to include only the objects that must change together atomically — and that set is almost always smaller than developers initially think.

sections.title: The Gatekeeper: How the Aggregate Root Enforces Invariants
Reference by ID: Why Aggregates Must Not Hold Object References to Each Other
sections.content:
One of the most important aggregate design rules is that aggregates reference each other **by identity only**. An `Order` stores `CustomerId` — a Value Object wrapping the customer's identifier — not a `Customer` object reference. This seems like a minor decision, but it prevents three serious problems.

First, **loading cascades**. If `Order` holds a `Customer` object, loading an order means also loading the customer, and if the customer has a list of orders, you have a cycle that ORM lazy-loading obscures but does not solve. With ID references, each aggregate loads independently through its own repository.

Second, **lock contention**. If two aggregates hold object references to each other and both are modified in the same transaction, the database must lock rows in both tables. Under concurrency, this creates deadlocks or serialization failures. ID references mean each aggregate modifies only its own rows.

Third, **independent evolution**. When `Customer` and `Order` are separate aggregates with ID references, each can evolve its schema, add fields, or change its persistence strategy without affecting the other. The coupling between them is a stable identifier — the thinnest possible contract.

When you need data from another aggregate, load it through its repository in the application service: `Customer customer = customerRepository.findById(order.getCustomerId())`. This makes the cross-aggregate dependency explicit and visible in the use case code, rather than hidden behind a lazy-loaded object graph.

sections.title: The Small Aggregate Heuristic: Why Less Is Almost Always Right
sections.content:
Vaughn Vernon's most impactful recommendation is to **design small aggregates**. An aggregate should contain only the entities and value objects that must be immediately consistent after every mutation. If an `Order` and a `Customer` can tolerate temporary inconsistency — a customer's updated name does not need to be instantly reflected in existing orders — they should be separate aggregates.

Large aggregates cause three production problems. **Contention**: every operation on the aggregate locks the entire cluster, so two users adding different line items to the same order must be serialized. **Loading cost**: the aggregate loads as a unit, so a 200-line order loads all 200 lines even if the operation only checks the status. **Merge conflicts**: with optimistic locking (version columns), concurrent modifications to any part of the aggregate cause `OptimisticLockException` even when the changes do not actually conflict.

When two aggregates need coordinated changes — for example, submitting an `Order` should reserve `Inventory` — use **eventual consistency** via domain events rather than expanding the aggregate boundary. The `Order` fires an `OrderSubmittedEvent`, and an event handler in the Inventory context processes the reservation asynchronously. This eliminates cross-aggregate locking and reduces transaction scope.

For the rare cases where strong consistency is genuinely required across two aggregates (transferring money between two `Account` instances), model the operation as a domain service that loads both, performs the transfer, and saves both in a single transaction. Document these exceptions explicitly — if they proliferate, your aggregate boundaries likely need revision.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Aggregate = transactional consistency boundary** — the cluster of objects that must be immediately consistent after every state change; cross-aggregate consistency is eventual
- **Aggregate Root = single entry point** — all mutations go through the root's methods; direct access to internal entities (`orderLine.setPrice()`) bypasses invariant enforcement
- **Small aggregates by default** — include only what must be immediately consistent; `Order` + `OrderLine`s yes; `Order` + `Customer` no — customer data is not part of the order invariant
- **Reference by ID across aggregates** — `order.customerId` (a `CustomerId` value object) not `order.customer`; object references create eager loading, large transactions, and tight coupling
- **Eventual consistency between aggregates** — when `Order` is submitted, it raises `OrderSubmittedEvent`; the Inventory aggregate handles it separately; brief inconsistency is the trade-off for small, high-concurrency aggregates

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
An Aggregate is a transactional consistency boundary — a cluster of domain objects that must remain consistent with each other after every state change. The Aggregate Root is the single entry point: all interactions with objects inside the aggregate must go through the root, not directly to the internal members.

**Why aggregates exist**
- An `Order` total must always equal the sum of its line prices — this is an invariant that spans multiple objects; the aggregate enforces it by controlling all mutations in one place
- Without an aggregate boundary, any service can call `orderLine.setPrice(0)` directly and produce an inconsistent state — the order total is now wrong and there's no place in the code responsible for checking it
- The aggregate root's methods are the invariant enforcement point — `order.addLine(product, quantity)` recalculates the total; no caller can modify a line without going through the order

**Sizing aggregates — the biggest design decision**
- Small aggregates are the right default — include only the objects that must be immediately consistent, not objects that are merely related
- An `Order` aggregate includes `OrderLine`s because the total invariant spans them; it does not include `Customer` because customer data is not part of that invariant
- Large aggregates cause contention: two concurrent operations on the same aggregate must serialize because they modify the same consistency unit; small aggregates mean more parallelism

**Cross-aggregate consistency**
- Aggregates reference each other by ID, not by object reference — `order.customerId` (a `CustomerId` value object), not `order.customer` (a `Customer` object)
- When an invariant spans two aggregates, use eventual consistency via domain events — `OrderSubmittedEvent` triggers a `ReservationRequested` command in the Inventory aggregate; they may be briefly inconsistent, but will converge

The hardest part of DDD design is aggregate sizing — too large and you have contention and bloat; too small and invariants leak into the application layer.

questions.question: What are Domain Events in DDD and how do you implement them in Java?
questions.title: Domain Events — What They Are and How to Implement Them
questions.direct_answer: A Domain Event is a record of something significant that happened in the domain — OrderPlaced, PaymentReceived, CustomerPromoted. Events are immutable facts in past tense. They decouple the source of a change from its side effects (sending emails, updating other aggregates, triggering workflows) and enable eventual consistency between Bounded Contexts.

sections.title: The Side-Effect Coupling Problem That Domain Events Solve
sections.content:
When an order is submitted, the system needs to reserve inventory, initiate payment, send a confirmation email, and update analytics. Without domain events, the use case that submits the order must know about all of these concerns — it becomes a God method with direct dependencies on inventory, payment, email, and analytics services. Adding a new side effect means modifying the order submission code, which violates the Open-Closed Principle and creates a fragile orchestration point.

Domain Events invert this coupling. The Order aggregate fires an `OrderSubmittedEvent` — an immutable fact named in past tense — and interested parties subscribe independently. The Order does not know or care what happens in response. Inventory reacts by reserving stock. Notifications react by sending email. Analytics reacts by recording the conversion. Each handler is independent, testable, and deployable without touching the order submission logic.

The critical implementation detail that separates a production-quality approach from a naive one is **when events are published**. The aggregate should never call `ApplicationEventPublisher.publish()` directly — that couples the domain to Spring. Instead, the aggregate collects events internally, and the application service publishes them **after the aggregate is successfully persisted**. This ordering — save first, publish second — prevents the system from announcing something that did not actually persist.

sections.title: Step 1 — Model Events as Immutable Records and Collect Them in the Aggregate
Step 2 — Publish After Save: The Ordering That Prevents Data Loss
Step 3 — Cross-Service Delivery: The Outbox Pattern for Guaranteed Delivery
sections.content:
For cross-service communication — telling a different microservice that an order was submitted — publishing directly to Kafka after the database commit has a fatal flaw: if the application crashes between the database commit and the Kafka publish, the event is lost. The Outbox pattern solves this by making event publication transactional.

Instead of publishing directly to Kafka, the application service writes domain events to an `outbox_events` table in the **same database transaction** as the aggregate save. A separate process — the Outbox Relay — polls the outbox table and publishes unpublished events to Kafka, marking them as published afterward. Since the aggregate save and the event write share a database transaction, they are atomically consistent.

Debezium, a CDC (Change Data Capture) tool, eliminates the polling overhead entirely. It tails the database's transaction log and publishes outbox rows to Kafka in near-real-time. The Debezium Outbox Router transforms rows into properly structured Kafka messages with headers for aggregate ID, event type, and payload — no custom polling code required.

Downstream consumers **must be idempotent** because at-least-once delivery means events may arrive more than once. Store processed event IDs in a `processed_events` table and check before handling, or design handlers to be naturally idempotent — creating a shipment for an already-shipped order is a no-op. This idempotency requirement exists regardless of the transport mechanism.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Domain events = past-tense facts from the aggregate** — `OrderSubmittedEvent` not `SubmitOrderCommand`; immutable, carrying only the data consumers need
- **Collect inside the aggregate, publish after save** — `order.submit()` adds the event internally; the use case calls `eventPublisher.publish(order.pullDomainEvents())` after `repository.save(order)` succeeds
- **Never inject `ApplicationEventPublisher` into the aggregate** — that couples the domain to Spring; aggregates collect events, use cases publish them
- **In-process events disappear on crash** — between save and publish, a crash loses the event; the Outbox pattern fixes this: write event to an `outbox` table in the same transaction, poll and forward to Kafka
- **Event consumers are decoupled** — inventory, email, analytics each listen for `OrderSubmittedEvent`; the order use case knows none of them; adding a new consumer requires no change to the order domain

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Domain Events solve the side-effect coupling problem. When an order is submitted, the system needs to reserve inventory, send a confirmation email, and update analytics. Without domain events, the use case that submits the order must directly call inventory, email, and analytics services — it becomes a God method where every downstream system is explicitly coupled to the order submission logic.

**What a domain event is**
- A Domain Event represents something that happened in the domain — past tense, immutable — `OrderSubmittedEvent`, `PaymentConfirmedEvent`, `ItemShippedEvent`; it carries the ID and facts needed by consumers
- The event is created and collected inside the aggregate during a state transition — `order.submit()` adds `new OrderSubmittedEvent(order.id(), order.customerId(), order.total())` to an internal events collection
- The use case publishes collected events *after* saving the aggregate — this ensures events are only published if the aggregate was successfully persisted

**The collect-and-publish pattern**
- The aggregate root has a `List<DomainEvent> domainEvents` collection — state-changing methods add events; the root does not publish directly (that would couple it to Spring's `ApplicationEventPublisher`)
- After `orderRepository.save(order)`, the use case calls `eventPublisher.publish(order.pullDomainEvents())` — atomically: save first, then publish
- Spring's `ApplicationEventPublisher` is fine for in-process events; for cross-service reliability, use the Outbox pattern: write events to an `outbox` table in the same database transaction, then poll and publish to Kafka

**The Outbox pattern for reliability**
- In-process events disappear if the process crashes between save and publish — the Outbox solves this: the event row is committed with the aggregate in the same transaction; a background poller reads and forwards to Kafka
- This is exactly how Debezium CDC works — it reads the `outbox` table's transaction log and publishes each row as a Kafka message; at-least-once delivery is guaranteed

questions.question: How does the Repository pattern work in Domain-Driven Design?
questions.title: Repository Pattern in Domain-Driven Design
questions.direct_answer: In DDD, a Repository provides the illusion that aggregates live in an in-memory collection. The domain defines the Repository interface with domain-language query methods. There is exactly one Repository per Aggregate Root. The Repository hides all persistence details — the domain model speaks to a collection-like interface and has no knowledge of SQL, JPA, or any database technology.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding that the Repository is a domain concept (collection abstraction), not just a data access pattern
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Having multiple repositories for the same aggregate, or having repositories for non-aggregate-root entities
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the 'collection-oriented' vs 'persistence-oriented' repository styles and when each is appropriate in Java

sections.title: The Collection Illusion: Why a DDD Repository Is Not a DAO
sections.content:
Most Java developers encounter the Repository pattern through Spring Data's `JpaRepository` and conclude that a Repository is just a data access object with a nicer name. This misunderstanding produces codebases where every table has a repository, query methods expose SQL-like semantics (`findByStatusAndPaymentStatus`), and the domain layer is riddled with persistence concerns.

In DDD, Evans describes the Repository as something fundamentally different: it provides the **illusion of an in-memory collection** of aggregates. You "add" an aggregate to the collection. You "find" it by domain-meaningful criteria. You let the collection handle all persistence details behind the scenes. The key constraints: there is exactly **one Repository per Aggregate Root** (not per entity, not per table), the interface is defined in the **domain layer** (not the infrastructure layer), and the query methods express **domain semantics** rather than database operations.

This means `OrderLineRepository` should not exist — `OrderLine` is internal to the `Order` aggregate and is accessed by loading the `Order` through `OrderRepository`. It also means the interface says `findSubmittedOrdersAwaitingPayment()`, not `findByStatusAndPaymentStatus(SUBMITTED, PENDING)`. The first speaks the domain's Ubiquitous Language; the second leaks the data model into the domain interface.

The distinction between a DDD Repository and a generic DAO is not academic — it has direct consequences for how the codebase evolves. A DAO exposes CRUD operations for a single table, encouraging callers to think in terms of SQL. A DDD Repository exposes aggregate-level operations, which means loading an `Order` always includes its `OrderLines` as a consistent unit. This aggregate-loading semantic is what maintains invariant enforcement across reads and writes — something a per-table DAO cannot guarantee. When you load an Order through a DDD Repository, you get the complete aggregate with all its invariants intact and ready to be enforced by the root.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The DDD Repository pattern is best understood through Evans' original metaphor: it provides the illusion of an in-memory collection of aggregates. You put an `Order` in, you get an `Order` out by searching with domain criteria — the repository hides whether that involves SQL, a document store, or a cache.

**What makes a DDD Repository different from a DAO**
- A DAO (Data Access Object) is organized around database operations — `findByStatusAndCreatedAtBefore(String status, Instant cutoff)` is a DAO method; it exposes SQL thinking in domain language
- A Repository is organized around the aggregate's lifecycle — `findPendingOrdersOlderThan(Duration age)` is a Repository method; it speaks the domain language the business uses
- The interface lives in the domain layer and the business defines its methods; a DAO lives in the infrastructure layer and the database schema defines its methods

**One repository per aggregate root**
- This is the most violated DDD rule in practice: one `OrderRepository`, never an `OrderLineRepository` — line items are accessed only through the `Order` aggregate, never directly
- Separate repositories for aggregate internals break the consistency boundary: a service with direct `OrderLine` access can bypass the `Order`'s invariant enforcement
- If you frequently need to load a line item without its parent order, that's a signal that the aggregate boundary is wrong — perhaps `OrderLine` should be its own aggregate

**Collection-oriented vs persistence-oriented style**
- Collection-oriented (Evans' original): `repository.add(order)` to persist, `repository.get(id)` to retrieve — modified aggregates are tracked automatically by a Unit of Work pattern; JPA's `EntityManager` behaves this way
- Persistence-oriented (pragmatic alternative): `repository.save(order)` for both insert and update — Spring Data's `JpaRepository.save()` is this style; no automatic change tracking; explicitly call save after modifying

questions.question: What is the difference between a Domain Service and an Application Service in DDD?
questions.title: Domain Services vs Application Services in DDD
questions.direct_answer: A Domain Service encapsulates business logic that does not naturally belong to any single Entity or Value Object — it speaks the domain language and has no framework dependencies. An Application Service orchestrates use cases: it loads aggregates, calls domain logic, handles transactions, and coordinates infrastructure. Application Services are thin orchestrators; Domain Services are pure business logic.

sections.title: The Anemic Domain Model Trap: Where Logic Lives Determines Your Architecture's Health
sections.content:
The most common failure mode in DDD codebases is the **anemic domain model** — entities that are nothing but data bags with getters and setters, while all business logic lives in service classes. This happens because developers put everything in Application Services without recognizing that some logic is genuinely domain logic that belongs deeper in the architecture.

The distinction is about **what the logic knows**. A Domain Service contains business rules that a domain expert would recognize and describe in their language — pricing calculations, transfer policies, fraud detection rules. It operates on domain objects (Entities and Value Objects) and has zero framework dependencies. An Application Service orchestrates the use case: it loads aggregates from repositories, calls domain logic, persists changes, publishes events, and manages the transaction boundary. It knows about infrastructure but not about business rules.

The litmus test: could a domain expert read this code and understand it? If the logic is about calculating whether a funds transfer exceeds daily limits, that is domain logic — it belongs in a `FundsTransferDomainService` or on the entities themselves. If the logic is about loading accounts from the database, calling the transfer, and saving the results, that is orchestration — it belongs in an Application Service.

A useful mental model: Domain Services speak the **Ubiquitous Language** and operate purely on domain objects passed as parameters. Application Services speak Java and Spring — they know about `@Transactional`, repository calls, event publishers, and request/response DTOs. When you see a service class that mixes both vocabularies — business `if/else` alongside `repository.save()` — it is doing two jobs, and the business logic should be extracted into a Domain Service or pushed onto the entities.

sections.content:
The most common failure in DDD codebases is putting everything in Application Services and ending up with an anemic domain model — entities that are data bags, and services that are god classes. The distinction between Domain Services and Application Services determines where business rules live.

**Domain Services — business logic that doesn't belong on one aggregate**
- A Domain Service contains domain logic that a domain expert would recognize and describe — pricing calculations, transfer policies, fraud rules, tax computations — expressed in the Ubiquitous Language
- Use a Domain Service when the logic naturally involves multiple aggregates and cannot sensibly live on either one: `TransferService.transfer(sourceAccount, targetAccount, amount)` — the debit/credit rule spans both accounts
- Domain Services are plain Java classes with no Spring annotations — they can be instantiated with `new` in unit tests; they receive aggregates and value objects, operate on them, and return domain results

**Application Services — orchestration, not logic**
- The Application Service (Use Case Interactor) loads the aggregate from the repository, calls the domain method or domain service, persists the result, and publishes domain events — it orchestrates without containing business rules
- `@Transactional` belongs here, not in the domain service — the use case controls the transaction boundary; the domain service is called within that transaction
- Application Services are the boundary where technical concerns enter: the use case understands commands and queries, calls Spring or infrastructure ports, and translates results back to DTOs

**The practical test**
- Would a domain expert understand and validate this logic if you read it to them? → Domain Service or aggregate method
- Is this orchestration, security check, transaction management, or calling external services? → Application Service
- If a Domain Service starts injecting repositories or calling external APIs, it has leaked into Application Service territory

questions.title: Ubiquitous Language — What It Is and How to Build It
questions.direct_answer: Ubiquitous Language is the shared vocabulary used by both developers and domain experts within a Bounded Context. Every term in conversations, documentation, and code is the same — there is no translation layer between what business people say and what the code says. Establishing it requires continuous collaboration: Event Storming sessions, a living glossary, and ruthless refactoring when the model drifts from the language.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Creating a glossary in a wiki that nobody maintains, rather than reflecting the language directly in the code and keeping it alive through ongoing conversations
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Describe Event Storming as a concrete technique for discovering the Ubiquitous Language and the domain model collaboratively

sections.title: The Translation Tax: How Mismatched Vocabulary Creates Hidden Bugs
sections.content:
Every time a developer has to translate between what the business says and what the code says, information is lost. A domain expert says "we need to **assess** a claim." The developer writes `PolicyService.processRecord(Long policyId, int typeCode, BigDecimal amt)`. Three translations happened silently: "claim" became "record," "assess" became "process," and the domain types dissolved into primitives. When a bug report says "claims are being assessed incorrectly," the developer has to reverse-translate to find the relevant code — and the translation itself is where misunderstandings breed.

Evans' insight was that this friction is not inevitable — it is a **design failure**. Ubiquitous Language eliminates the translation layer by insisting that the same words appear in conversations, documentation, and code. When the domain expert says "assess a claim," the code reads `claimService.assessClaim(PolicyId policyId, ClaimType claimType, Money claimAmount)`. The domain expert can read the method signature and confirm it matches their mental model. The developer can discuss a bug report without translating terminology.

The language is scoped to a single Bounded Context — "Customer" in Sales has different vocabulary than "Customer" in Support, and that is by design.

sections.title: Discovery Through Event Storming: Where the Language Comes From
sections.content:
The most effective technique for discovering the Ubiquitous Language is **Event Storming**. In a workshop with domain experts, developers, and product managers, the team maps the domain as a timeline of events (things that happened), commands (what triggered them), aggregates (what handled them), and policies (what happens in response).

The vocabulary that emerges — event names like `ClaimAssessed`, `PolicyActivated`, `CoverageExpired` — becomes the Ubiquitous Language. These are not developer inventions; they came directly from the domain experts in the room. When the team later writes `ClaimAssessedEvent`, `Policy.activate()`, and `Coverage.expire()`, the code speaks the same language the business uses.

A **living glossary** maintained as a markdown file in the repository (not a wiki that drifts) bridges the gap between workshops and code. Each entry has the term, its definition, and the corresponding class or method. During code reviews, check whether new code introduces synonyms for existing terms — if a developer creates `PolicyHolder` when the glossary says `Insured`, flag it immediately.

sections.title: Maintaining the Language: When Terms Evolve, Code Must Follow
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Ubiquitous Language lives in code, not a wiki** — `policy.assess(claim)` not `processRecord(Long, int, BigDecimal)`; the method name must be the term domain experts use
- **Developed collaboratively** — developers and domain experts agree on terms together; the developer cannot invent technical synonyms for business concepts
- **Divergence is a design smell** — when the business says "assess" and the code says "process", a translation is happening somewhere; every reader must reverse-engineer the intent
- **Event Storming discovers the language** — collaborative workshops with sticky notes mapping commands, events, policies, and aggregates surface the real domain vocabulary and expose where language is ambiguous
- **The language evolves** — renaming `Account` to `Subscription` because that's what the business actually calls it is a legitimate refactoring; an outdated model name is a liability

sections.content:
Every time a developer translates between what the business says and what the code says, information is lost. A domain expert says "assess a claim"; the developer writes `PolicyService.processRecord(Long policyId, int typeCode, BigDecimal amt)`. Three translations happened silently — and every reader of that code must now reverse-engineer the intent. Ubiquitous Language eliminates the translation by requiring that the same words appear in conversations, documents, and code.

**What Ubiquitous Language means in practice**
- The language is developed collaboratively — developers and domain experts model the domain together, agree on precise terms, and write those exact terms in the code
- `policy.assess(Claim claim)` not `processRecord(Long policyId, int typeCode, BigDecimal amt)` — the method name, parameter types, and return type all use terms the domain expert would recognize and use themselves
- When the domain expert describes a concept and the developer writes something different, that divergence is a design smell — the model is drifting from reality

**Keeping the language alive**
- A glossary in a wiki is not enough — it goes stale immediately and nobody reads it; the language must live in the code itself, enforced through naming conventions and code review
- Event Storming is the most effective workshop format for discovering and agreeing on the Ubiquitous Language: domain experts and developers use sticky notes to map commands, domain events, policies, and aggregates in timeline order — disagreements about terms surface naturally
- The language changes over time as understanding deepens — renaming a class from `Account` to `Subscription` when that's what the business actually calls it is a legitimate refactoring, not just cosmetic

**The impact on team communication**
- When developers and domain experts use the same vocabulary, conversations become precise — "the claim was assessed and a payment was authorized" maps directly to the code without translation

questions.question: What is the Anti-Corruption Layer pattern in DDD and when do you use it?
questions.title: Anti-Corruption Layer Pattern in DDD
questions.direct_answer: An Anti-Corruption Layer (ACL) is a translation layer that protects your domain model from being corrupted by external models — legacy systems, third-party APIs, or other Bounded Contexts with different conceptual models. It translates foreign concepts into your domain's own language, so your domain model never needs to know about or adapt to the external system's design.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of strategic DDD and how to protect domain model integrity when integrating with legacy or third-party systems
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using foreign model types directly in domain code — letting Stripe's PaymentIntent or Salesforce's Contact bleed into your domain model
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Describe the components of an ACL (Facade, Translator, local model) and explain how it maps to Clean Architecture's interface adapter layer

sections.title: How External Systems Silently Corrupt Your Domain Model
sections.content:
Every non-trivial system integrates with things it does not control — third-party payment processors, legacy systems built in the 1990s, partner APIs with their own idiosyncratic models. Without deliberate protection, foreign concepts seep into your domain model gradually and irreversibly. Stripe's `PaymentIntent` terminology appears in your payment domain. A legacy system's cryptic integer status codes become enums in your business logic. An external API's deeply nested error structure gets reflected in your exception hierarchy.

This corruption is insidious because each individual integration shortcut seems harmless — "why not just use Stripe's `PaymentIntent` class directly? It already has the fields we need." But over time, your domain model becomes a patchwork of external system conventions. Changing payment processors means rewriting domain logic, not just adapters. Testing requires mocking third-party client libraries. Your domain's vocabulary becomes a mix of your own language and every vendor's terminology.

The Anti-Corruption Layer creates a **firewall** between your domain and the external world. On one side is the external system with its model. On the other is your domain with its model. The ACL translates in both directions — converting your domain types to the external system's format on the way out, and converting external responses back to your domain types on the way in. Your domain model never imports, references, or adapts to any external system's classes.

sections.title: The Three-Part Structure: Port, Adapter, and Translator
The Replaceability Payoff: Swapping Vendors Without Touching Domain Logic
sections.content:
The ACL's most tangible benefit appears when you need to replace an external system. Without an ACL, switching from Stripe to Braintree means finding every place Stripe's types appear in your codebase — domain logic, use cases, error handling, test mocks — and rewriting all of them. With an ACL, the change is surgical: write a new `BraintreePaymentGatewayAdapter implements PaymentGateway`, deploy it, and the domain model is untouched.

This maps directly to Clean Architecture's **Interface Adapter** layer and Hexagonal Architecture's **Secondary Adapter**. The pattern is the same regardless of terminology: the domain defines its needs through an interface (output port), and the infrastructure provides the implementation that translates and isolates.

The ACL is also the natural testing boundary. Your domain tests mock the `PaymentGateway` interface — they never need to mock Stripe's HTTP client or parse Stripe's JSON responses. Integration tests for the adapter itself can use Stripe's test mode or WireMock to verify the translation logic. This separation means domain tests run in milliseconds and adapter tests can run against the real API in a CI pipeline without coupling the two test suites.

sections.title: When to Build an ACL vs When to Conform
sections.content:
Not every integration justifies an Anti-Corruption Layer. Building an ACL adds a translation layer, a mapper, and interface definitions — real work with ongoing maintenance cost. The alternative is the **Conformist** pattern: adopt the external system's model directly and design your domain around it.

Conformist is the right choice when the external model is reasonable and you have no leverage to change it. If you are building a Salesforce integration and your domain is fundamentally organized around Salesforce's concepts, translating back and forth adds friction without value. Conform to Salesforce's `Contact`, `Opportunity`, and `Lead` vocabulary and save the engineering effort.

The ACL is the right choice when any of these conditions hold: the external system's model is a **poor fit** for your domain (legacy systems with cryptic codes), you need **replaceability** (payment processors, email providers), or the external model **changes frequently** and you want to absorb those changes in one place rather than across your codebase. In practice, I default to building an ACL for any third-party API integration because the cost of the translation layer is small compared to the cost of vendor lock-in when it eventually matters.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **ACL = deliberate protection from foreign models** — Stripe's `PaymentIntent` should never appear in your domain; the ACL translates it to your `PaymentConfirmation` at the boundary
- **Three components** — Facade (adapter implementing the domain port), Translator (maps external model ↔ domain model), Local model (your domain's representation of the concept)
- **The port interface is the contract** — `PaymentGateway.charge(Money, PaymentMethod)` is yours; Stripe is just one implementation behind the ACL; switching providers changes only the adapter
- **Third-party models change** — Stripe deprecates APIs, Salesforce renames fields; with an ACL, the blast radius is one class; without it, the external change propagates through the entire domain
- **ACL maps to Clean Architecture's interface adapter layer** — the ACL pattern and Clean Architecture's outer adapter ring are the same concept with different names; they're complementary, not competing

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Every non-trivial system integrates with things it does not control — Stripe, legacy ERP systems, partner APIs, other teams' services. Without deliberate protection, foreign concepts seep into your domain model and permanently reshape it. Stripe's `PaymentIntent`, Salesforce's `Contact`, a legacy system's `CUST_ID` — if these leak into your domain, your model starts speaking the external system's language, not yours.

**What the Anti-Corruption Layer does**
- The ACL sits at the integration boundary — it contains a Facade (adapts the external API's interface), a Translator (maps the external model to your domain model), and a local domain model (your representation of the external concept)
- Your domain calls `paymentGateway.charge(order.total(), customer.paymentMethod())` — the ACL translates that into Stripe's API structure, calls Stripe, and maps `PaymentIntent` back to your domain's `PaymentConfirmation`
- The domain never imports Stripe's SDK or speaks Stripe's vocabulary — when Stripe changes their API or you switch to Braintree, only the ACL adapter changes

**Components of an ACL in Java**
- Facade: `StripePaymentGatewayAdapter implements PaymentGateway` — the adapter behind the domain port interface; Spring wires it in as the `PaymentGateway` implementation
- Translator: converts `StripePaymentIntent` → `PaymentConfirmation`, or `SalesforceLead` → `Customer`; these are explicit mapping classes, not auto-mapping frameworks
- Local model: `PaymentConfirmation`, `CustomerProfile` — your domain's representation; shaped by what your domain needs, not what Stripe provides

**When you need an ACL**
- Third-party APIs with their own rich models (Stripe, Twilio, Salesforce) — their model will change; the ACL contains the blast radius
- Legacy systems with database-centric, cryptic field names — the ACL translates `CUST_ID`, `ORD_STS_CD`, `AMT_DUE` into meaningful domain concepts
- Other teams' bounded contexts — even internal services may have models that don't align with yours; an ACL defines the explicit translation at the boundary

questions.question: How do you implement DDD tactical patterns in a Spring Boot application?
questions.title: DDD Tactical Patterns with Spring Boot — Practical Recipe
questions.direct_answer: Implementing DDD tactical patterns in Spring Boot requires deliberate structure: domain objects are pure Java (no Spring/JPA), repositories are interfaces defined in the domain layer, JPA entities are separate infrastructure classes mapped by adapters, Spring wires everything together via @Configuration classes. Spring is an implementation detail, not a participant in the domain model.

interviewer_intent.testing: Ability to translate DDD concepts into a working Spring Boot codebase — bridging theory and practice
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Annotating domain classes with @Entity and @Service, which couples the domain model directly to Spring and JPA
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show the full stack from aggregate to REST endpoint with explicit separation between domain, application, and infrastructure layers

sections.title: The Annotation Discipline: Why Your Domain Must Never See @Entity or @Component
sections.content:
The most common mistake when implementing DDD in Spring Boot is reaching for `@Entity`, `@Service`, and `@Component` on domain classes. This feels natural — Spring rewards annotation-driven development, and JPA requires `@Entity` for persistence. But the moment your `Order` aggregate carries `@Entity`, your domain model is coupled to JPA's constraints: mandatory no-arg constructors, mutable setters for proxy hydration, `@Column` annotations on domain fields, and a class hierarchy shaped by ORM requirements rather than business rules.

The disciplined approach treats Spring as the **infrastructure concern** it is. The tactical patterns — Aggregates, Value Objects, Domain Events, Repositories — are implemented in pure Java. They compile and test without Spring on the classpath. Spring provides dependency injection, transaction management, JPA, and HTTP — all in the outer layers. The domain model never imports `org.springframework`.

This separation requires explicit wiring: a `@Configuration` class that creates domain services and use cases as `@Bean` definitions, a repository adapter that bridges the domain's `OrderRepository` interface to JPA's `JpaRepository`, and a mapper that translates between domain aggregates and JPA entities. The extra code pays for itself in testability — domain logic tests run in milliseconds without a Spring context, database, or transaction manager.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Implementing DDD in Spring Boot is fundamentally about discipline over where Spring annotations appear. The domain model — aggregates, value objects, domain services — is pure Java. The moment `@Entity`, `@Service`, or `@Transactional` appears on a domain class, the domain is coupled to a framework and the architecture begins to erode.

**The full stack — layer by layer**
- Domain layer: `Order` aggregate (no annotations), `OrderLine` value object (Java record), `OrderId` value object (record wrapping UUID), `OrderRepository` interface — pure Java, zero framework imports
- Application layer: `SubmitOrderUseCase` implementing `SubmitOrderInputPort` — orchestrates the use case, calls domain methods and repository ports, publishes domain events, owns `@Transactional`
- Infrastructure layer: `OrderEntity` (annotated with `@Entity`), `SpringDataJpaOrderRepository extends JpaRepository<OrderEntity, Long>`, `JpaOrderRepositoryAdapter implements OrderRepository` — maps between JPA entities and domain objects
- Presentation layer: `OrderController @RestController` — maps HTTP request to command DTO, calls input port, maps result to response DTO

**The two Order classes**
- `Order` (domain): pure Java, enforces invariants through methods like `submit()`, `cancel()`, `addLine()`, carries `List<DomainEvent>` for collected events
- `OrderEntity` (JPA): carries `@Entity`, `@Table`, `@Column`, `@OneToMany` for Spring Data; shaped by the database schema, not business rules
- The `JpaOrderRepositoryAdapter` translates between them — `toDomain(OrderEntity)` and `toEntity(Order)` methods; tested with `@DataJpaTest` independently of the use case

**Testing the full stack**
- Use case: `new SubmitOrderUseCase(mock(OrderRepository.class), mock(EventPublisher.class))` — milliseconds, no Spring
- Adapter: `@DataJpaTest` with `JpaOrderRepositoryAdapter` — real JPA, H2 or Testcontainers, tests the mapping
- Controller: `@WebMvcTest` with mocked input port — tests HTTP contract without business logic

questions.question: What is Strategic DDD and what are the key Context Mapping patterns?
questions.title: Strategic DDD: Context Mapping Patterns
questions.direct_answer: Strategic DDD deals with the high-level organization of a large domain into Bounded Contexts and the relationships between them. Context Mapping patterns describe these relationships: Shared Kernel (shared model), Customer-Supplier (one feeds the other), Conformist (downstream adopts upstream's model), Anti-Corruption Layer (downstream protects its model), Published Language (open protocol), and Separate Ways (no integration).

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Knowing only the tactical patterns (aggregates, value objects) without understanding how Bounded Contexts integrate — the strategic side is often neglected
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connect context mapping patterns to concrete microservice integration styles: REST APIs, domain events over Kafka, shared databases

sections.title: Beyond Aggregates and Value Objects: The Architectural Decisions That Actually Determine System Health
sections.content:
Most developers who learn DDD focus exclusively on tactical patterns — aggregates, entities, value objects, domain events. These are important, but they operate at the object-design level within a single Bounded Context. Strategic DDD operates one level up: **how do you carve a large, complex business domain into Bounded Contexts, and how should those contexts integrate with each other?**

The Context Map is the key artifact. It is a diagram showing every Bounded Context in the system and the **relationship pattern** between each pair that integrates. These patterns are not documentation decorations — they encode the power dynamic between teams, the level of model coupling, and the integration mechanism. Choosing the wrong pattern for a relationship creates ongoing friction: teams blocked on each other, models corrupted by foreign concepts, or integration contracts that change without notice.

The patterns fall into three categories: **cooperative** (both teams collaborate on the integration), **defensive** (one team protects itself from the other's model), and **independent** (no integration at all). Understanding which pattern fits each relationship is one of the highest-leverage architectural decisions in a system with multiple Bounded Contexts — it determines how much autonomy each team has, how tightly coupled the systems become, and how painful changes will be over time.

sections.title: Cooperative Patterns: Shared Kernel and Customer-Supplier
sections.content:
**Shared Kernel** means two Bounded Contexts share a small, explicitly agreed-upon subset of the domain model — typically value objects like `Money`, `DateRange`, or `CustomerId` that genuinely belong to both contexts. The shared code lives in a separate library that both teams depend on. Changes to the shared kernel require coordination: both teams must agree before any modification, and the library is versioned carefully.

The discipline required is keeping the kernel **minimal**. If the shared library grows beyond a handful of types, it signals that the context boundaries need redrawing — you are creating a hidden unified model through the back door. In practice, a shared kernel works well for fundamental value types that are domain-wide (money, identifiers, date ranges) and poorly for anything more complex.

**Customer-Supplier** describes a relationship where the upstream context produces data or services that the downstream context consumes. The downstream team has negotiating power — they can request API changes, report bugs, and influence the upstream's roadmap. This is the healthiest pattern for internal teams that collaborate regularly.

In microservice terms, Customer-Supplier often manifests as a REST API with a defined contract, where the downstream team can open pull requests or tickets against the upstream's API. The upstream publishes a changelog and respects semantic versioning. Both teams understand the dependency and manage it actively.

sections.title: Defensive Patterns: Conformist and Anti-Corruption Layer
sections.content:
**Conformist** means the downstream team adopts the upstream's model without translation. You accept Salesforce's `Contact`, `Opportunity`, and `Lead` vocabulary as-is and design your internal model around it. This is pragmatic when the upstream model is reasonable, stable, and you have no leverage to change it. Building a translation layer would add engineering cost without meaningful benefit.

The risk of Conformist is **vendor lock-in**. Your domain vocabulary becomes the vendor's vocabulary. If the upstream changes its model (Salesforce renames a field, a legacy system changes status codes), the ripple effect hits your domain directly. Conformist works when the coupling cost is low and the stability is high.

**Anti-Corruption Layer** is the defensive alternative. The downstream builds a translation layer that converts the upstream's concepts into its own domain language. Your domain defines `PaymentGateway` with `Money` and `PaymentResult`; the ACL implements it by translating to/from Stripe's `PaymentIntent` and cent-based amounts. The domain never sees the external model.

The ACL is more work but provides replaceability (swap Stripe for Braintree by changing only the adapter), testability (mock the domain interface, not the HTTP client), and insulation from upstream model changes. **My default is to build an ACL for any third-party integration** — the translation cost is small compared to the long-term cost of vendor concepts embedded throughout the domain.

sections.title: Independence Patterns: Published Language, Open Host Service, and Separate Ways
sections.content:
**Published Language** means both contexts integrate through a well-documented, versioned protocol that belongs to neither context's internal model. Avro schemas for Kafka events, OpenAPI specifications for REST APIs, or Protobuf definitions for gRPC — the shared contract is the integration language. Neither team exposes its internal model; they communicate through the published format.

This pattern scales to many consumers. An **Open Host Service** is a context that publishes a formal API designed for external consumption. Multiple downstream contexts can integrate with it without each needing a bilateral relationship. The upstream invests in API design, versioning, and documentation as a first-class concern.

**Separate Ways** is the decision not to integrate at all. Two contexts solve overlapping problems independently, with no shared code, no events, and no API calls. This seems wasteful — why implement user management in two places? — but sometimes the integration cost exceeds the duplication cost. If two teams need slightly different user models and would spend more time coordinating integration contracts than building independently, Separate Ways is the correct choice.

In practice, drawing the Context Map early and annotating each relationship with its pattern forces the team to make these decisions consciously. Without the map, teams discover their integration patterns accidentally — usually when one team's deployment breaks another team's system. The Context Map turns implicit coupling into explicit, manageable relationships.

Connecting these to microservice implementation: Shared Kernel becomes a shared Maven dependency with careful version management. Customer-Supplier becomes a REST API with SLAs and changelogs. Published Language becomes Avro/Protobuf schemas in a schema registry. The strategic pattern determines the integration mechanism, not the other way around.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Context mapping = how Bounded Contexts integrate** — the pattern you choose determines team coupling, autonomy, and blast radius when one context changes
- **ACL for external and legacy systems** — never let Stripe's `PaymentIntent` or a legacy system's `CUST_ID` reach your domain; always translate at the ACL boundary
- **Customer-Supplier for platform teams** — the platform (upstream supplier) defines the API; the product team (downstream customer) adapts; the supplier owns the contract
- **Published Language = explicit event schema** — Avro schemas in Kafka or OpenAPI specs are the shared vocabulary; both sides agree before changing it; the schema is the integration contract
- **Domain events over Kafka are the clean integration** — `OrderSubmittedEvent` from the Order context, consumed by Inventory asynchronously; no shared database, no direct service call, no tight coupling

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Strategic DDD operates at the architecture level — how do you carve a large, complex business domain into manageable Bounded Contexts, and how do those contexts integrate? While tactical patterns give you well-designed objects within a single context, strategic DDD determines the team boundaries, ownership, and integration contracts between contexts.

**The core context mapping patterns**
- **Partnership**: two teams collaborate closely, coordinate releases together — tight coupling by choice; works when teams move at the same pace and trust is high; breaks down at scale
- **Shared Kernel**: a shared library or package that both contexts depend on — a common vocabulary or utility; the teams must agree before modifying it; becomes a coordination bottleneck if overused
- **Customer-Supplier**: one team is the supplier (upstream) and another is the customer (downstream) — the supplier's API is the contract; the customer adapts to it; common with platform teams
- **Conformist**: the downstream team simply accepts and conforms to the upstream model rather than translating — cheaper but introduces the upstream model's vocabulary into the downstream domain
- **Anti-Corruption Layer (ACL)**: the downstream builds a translation layer to protect its model from the upstream — correct but costly; use when the upstream model is hostile or unstable

**Integrating Bounded Contexts in practice**
- Published Language: a well-documented, versioned event schema shared between contexts — Avro schemas in Kafka, OpenAPI specs for REST; the language is explicit and evolved by agreement
- Open Host Service: the upstream exposes a stable API that any downstream can consume — REST or gRPC with versioning; the upstream protects its consumers through backward compatibility
- Domain events via Kafka: `OrderSubmittedEvent` published by the Order context consumed by the Inventory context — asynchronous, decoupled; the event schema is the Published Language

**Choosing a pattern**
- Close teams, shared codebase: Shared Kernel or Partnership
- Platform team serving product teams: Customer-Supplier with Open Host Service
- Legacy or external system: ACL always — never conform to a hostile upstream model
